posts.author: Samolexie
posts.body:
There is something I heard a lot of times, especially but not only in YouTube video, is that you should not use RTP assets in your game. Sometimes, it even go as far as "don't make your game look like it was made with RPG Maker". I just don't understand this statement. What's the point of using RPG Maker if it's to make it look like something else? Just use another engine then?
Usually, the arguments revolve around the fact that people won't buy because RTP games are bad games (how so?). But, one of the appeal of RPG Maker is the RTP. Way less people would buy the software if it didn't have basic ressources included (I think). I mean, you bought them with the software, so you would like to use them, but you shouldn't because some people decided that RTP are bad?
In the end, either you need to buy DLC ressources, that you have also seen dozens of times, or you need to create your own ressources. Which means you have to draw characters, compose music, make pixel art, draw UI, etc yourself or find a team to do it if you can't yourself. I think it's a lot of unnecessary efforts just to appeal to that "RTP is bad" statement. Well, if you WANT to make custom things and all, just go, but I don't like to be somewhat forced to do it if I'm fine with RTP or well known DLC/community ressources just so people start thinking that my game might have the potential to be good.
Did I miss the point? Am I overthinking it? What do you think about this?

posts.author: AquaEcho
posts.body:
The RTP is associated with low effort/quality games because the creator couldnt be bothered to change the stock assets. If you're using some other premade assets, at least you made some minimal effort to consider a stylistic theming and pick an asset pack to match it. That would still be considered a lazy asset flip by some but a step above the RTP.
That said, unless someone is familiar with RPG Maker or plays a lot of indie games they might not even recognize your assets.
There are successful games that use the RTP like To The Moon or premade asset packs like Crystal Project that uses Time Fantasy. There are also many games that have full custom art only to have only a couple dozen people play them.
There's also premade asset packs I've never seen anyone use (at least here). Some are overused like Time Fantasy or Pop Horror but I've never seen Clockwork Raven for example.

posts.author: Aerosys
posts.body:
I've seen many games using RTP that also had some intermediate mapping, maybe parallax mapping, or other improvements such as lighting or fog effects (of course, that doesn't mean that just because you add such effects you would automatically get a great game). So when you can prove on your screenshots that you know how to design good maps then it's totally fine to use RTP in my opinion. I regularly see excellent screenshots using RTP (sometimes with tiny adjustments in the tilesets).
Well, it's almost a fact that there are many RPG Maker games that were either lazily or otherwise poorly designed, so people often link RTP games with bad games.

posts.author: Andar
posts.body:
In the earlier years of Steam, when you could get a game published without paying anything or with only token costs, Steam was flooded with a lot of "no-effort-games".
Basically people using the dungeon generator and perhaps a week of work to put together something that pretends to be a game. And then publishing it in the hope that more than a dozen people buy it.
It didn't just happen to the RPG-Makers, it actually happened with any cheap or free game engine ever available - but due to the distinguished "look" of the RTP and the ease of use of the makers, it was much more problematic here.
To use the RTP successfully today basically requires you to either put in the efford to become good at mapping and showing that your game is the result of work that way, or to use a different set of aesthetics.
But I think the storm against RTP has mostly passed - at least compared to what was said at that time when Steam was flooded with crap RM games.

posts.author: ZimXero
posts.body:
RTP is one of the best tile sets
available for fantasy games.  What throws me off (immersion and confidence in the game) is when the interface is mostly default, the icons are mostly default, or the first enemies I encounter are from the default enemy set.  Also, typos and bad grammar at the start of a game are a sign to quit before it's too late.  Also, if a game has less than 20 hours of gameplay, I won't touch it unless it's award winning.  This is because I don't want to invest the time and effort into learning the game system, knowing the characters and story, just to have it end abruptly soon after.
I have combat at the top of my list.  If the combat isn't interesting to play... then just skip it or make it story based.  World is number 2... cause it's gotta be worth the walk and it's gotta be worth fighting for. Interface is number 3... a bad interface system ruins everything.  These 3 are the main frame of all games.  To me, story and characters are the texture that goes over the mainframe.   They can make an otherwise good game either legendary or lackluster.  They can't turn a junk game into a classic.
Bad games with a good sales presentations outnumber good games by about 5 to 1.   There are more good games around than a person can possibly play.  Because of this, many players have taken the shortcut of assuming RTP means the game ain't good enough to play.  They aren't wrong,... usually.

posts.author: sunhihi
posts.body:
It depends on whether you're planning to sell your game.
Using RTP (RPG Maker's default resources) can feel cheap to some people—kind of like using AI-generated images—but in reality, RTP is actually quite good. A lot of free resources on forums are based on RTP edits, and many of them are better than paid assets. Not using them at all is honestly a waste.
Of course, if your game's main selling point isn't the gameplay but rather some "beautiful images," then it's not such a big deal. That’s part of why RPG Maker is jokingly called an “eroge generator.”
Many people want to make games and earn money, but don’t want to spend on DLC, don’t know how to draw, and don’t know how to code. RPG Maker often claims that you can quickly make a game without needing any coding or art skills—so you end up with tons of games made entirely with default RTP assets. And that leads to a situation where people judge the game as unworthy just by its look and skip it entirely, never getting to the actual content.

You largely have three options;
Don't make a video game. There's multiple types of read-only media for stories out there if all you want is to write. It only makes sense to make it into a movie or tv show if visuals are important to your story and into a game if interaction is important to the story.
Work on a team. Everyone can work to their strengths. In fact, there are people on this site who excel at all sorts of things in making games but have no idea how to do anything story-related and want writers.
Focus on your writing as the focal point of your game. Embrace that it is your strength and let the writing carry the entire game. The point of even having an RTP (and premade maps, database, etc) is to help you. I
guarantee
you could make a game worth playing with everything being default assets if the story was good enough, plus there's a lot of tutorials around the site (and other places) to help you learn how to map, how to figure out your combat system, etc. I'm pretty sure people in this very thread could point you to well-made RTP games that work because of their story.
Literally the one thing RPG Maker does not give you is a script for your game. And it sounds like that's exactly the thing you want to do.

posts.author: M.I.A.

I really love the RTP that comes with the engines. Do they cover everything? No. Are they exactly what I wanted sometimes? Here and there. But.. does having the RTP allow me to focus on my personal favorite part of this whole process by taking the need for basic graphics off my plate? Absolutely. Does the RTP give me an idea of what additional resources I might need to look for/purchase to get the sometimes specific things I want for my game? Yes, and often custom creators design to match the RTP, increasing options. Is the RTP pretty easy to learn how to edit to my liking? Sometimes. My skills are very limited.
I can understand why some folks hate on the RTP though. And that's fine. They have other options! They can learn to build it all themselves or pay someone else who knows what they're doing.
RTP is a win/win for everyone.

posts.author: pawsplay
posts.body:
Let's say someone has enough knowledge to recognize my game was made in RPG Maker. That same person, if they are serious, will notice I have made edits and customized the assets. If they are truly interested in originality, they'll recognize the effort I've put in and give it a chance. My goal is to entertain. You know what doesn't come packaged in the RTP? You! Your ideas, your thoughts and feelings, your dreams, your unique touch.
If you were really into surf rock, and you went to a concert with a surf rock band, and they started playing, and you said, "Wow, that sounds exactly like some surf rock music," is that a criticism? It's only a bad thing if they don't add something new and original. And by something, I don't mean a lot, just something differentiates this experience from others. A gift, from the creator, to the audience. It is a whole lot more important to do something with earnestness and energy and love than to worry about technical innovations or virtuosity.
The worst thing that can happen to a creative is to become self-conscious about what they love, to not recognize the beauty in what they love because they love it.
EDIT: I also want to mention something else. I am a failed artist. I can't draw. I tried, and at the end of the day, I recognized that the pace of improvement I was making was really weak compared to my peers, and I began to perceive I might have a definite ceiling to my ability. I have family members who have a lot of ability, who started off better and learned faster, and it made me realize art was not going to be my thing. But along the way, I studied art, intensely. So in that sense I have a leg up on people who don't know art. But I'm not going to draw a lot of assets. What I can do, with great patience and with a clear vision of what I want to accomplish, is make edits. I don't have to rely on other people to do simple things, because I've developed confidence in the simple things I can do. It's fine to rely on the RTP. It's fine to just edit it in minor ways. It's fine to use other people's edits, and custom resources. It's fine to pay for commercially made assets. And it's fine to hire custom assets. There are many paths. Making a game is itself an undertaking, something most people won't try, and the majority of which who do try, won't finish. The majority who finish won't make something all that great. Just finishing a game is a titanic accomplishment. Making the cool thing is what's important. No one person has *all* the skills needed to make a game, to an expert level; we lean on our strengths, and when they aren't sufficient to reach our goals, we lean on the help of others.

posts.author: Avery
posts.body:
Maybe one day I write a full and long sorted post about good/bad RTP, but I just pulled out some other things I made in the past.
In this gif you see two maps, both made to show the exact same area.
Both made with the RTP style.
For one I looked through freely available tiles and build a tileset (just copy and paste), for one I used RTP out of the box. You might guess which is which.
Another example, this time not the same map, just the same type of map.
One all default, one with freebies selected for the map.
The thing with RTP tilesets is, that it not only has some weird choices (and definitly some cases of really bad art), it trys to be everything at once and fails at it, due to the limited amount of stuff in the default tiles.
The placement is also off since the tiles are crammed in to fit the set best, not to line up with the environment best. And not everything goes with everything. The vibe and the settings as is are super limited.
But then again, it is the most versatile style, since there are so many people who made additonal things. While you cannot find everything, you can find a lot. And a lot of that is amazing as well. No matter if I need a more extensive frost cave set (with rounded walls) or a castle, someone has made it. Different types of in- and exterior that allow for diverse towns. Different plants for different biomes.
Not wanna bash certain packs, but depending which ones people use, their games end up looking the same, cause their forests are stuck to a very limited selection of trees, and their town to the few offered styles.
While with RTP, IF you put in the effort, you can combine something unique out of the existing abundance. After all, it is just copy and paste and a little colorgrading maybe.
There are tons of tutorials out there that focus on that specific style, which also helps with giving you the tools to build what you really want. And in my opinion, no style option will look good if used out of the box as is. Cause while RTP is just bad without edits, the other sets can be very repetive and boring due to their limitations. At least RTP is much easier to expand with less work, due to the existing resources out there.
I will also drop my list with tutorials that might help with making a prettier RTP styled game:
[mostly graphics]Avery's Tutorials - an overview and a good starting point
I have written a lot of Tutorials over the years, and to make it easier for you guys to find what you need, I set up this "hub" where you can overview and access them all! Some were written with a specific engine in mind, and while e.g. the water autotile tutorial only applys to MZ because of...

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
The stigma mostly has to do with "low effort games".  RPG Maker games tend to be seen, outside the community (and even within the community), as "low effort", because there's a lot of people who do not do or understand "game dev".  So, they pump out a game real quick, and try to make like $1 per sale on it.
The RTP is recognizable.  So, seeing it becomes a kind of "dog whistle" for quality.  At least to people who don't really look into things or tend to have weird standards.
I, for one, have begun using "quality of the lighting" in many AAA games to determine that "the rest of the game is garbage".  Because, AAA games are so frontloaded with graphics that literally everything else about the game suffers and is subpar at best (or done before, by a game 10 years older, far better).
When you try to avoid "low effort" and "low quality" games, whatever you can find that is "the same between them" becomes your dog whistle on them.  Pattern Recognition is a thing.  You've seen some of those in this thread already.  Poor grammar/spelling, run away from the game.  Default menus, run away.  The list goes on and on.
I, personally, don't immediately discount the RTP.  I want to see what the mapping looks like, first.  Because, frankly, no matter what tileset you're using, or how good it looks... if you are garbo at mapping with it... it won't save you anyway.  Then again, I also personally enjoy the aesthetic of the RTP in most of the makers (which is why I own them all and move assets freely between them).
After mapping, I tend to look to see what the advertisement page thinks is "important".  If anything regarding "Graphics" lands on that list, I tend to just disregard the game in general.  You want to advertise your artwork?  Open up a deviantart account.  I'm here for the game.  Advertise the game.
"Amazing Raytracing and realistic water effects!"
Ah, that's where your budget went.  That's where all your effort went.  No thank you.  If looking at pretty and realistic water/light beams were why I was here... I wouldn't be here.  I'd be out at the lake, doing some fishing.  Or hiking.
Save the "realistic graphics" for when the game console is wired into my central nervous system and I'm literally in the game.  Then, I'll care what it looks like, since it will matter to immersion.

posts.author: ZombieKidzRule
posts.body:
Your profile indicates that you primarily use VXA, which I own but have no real experience with, so my response will focus pretty much on my experiences with MZ.
I think the primary reason has already been mentioned multiple times. The RTP can be associated by some with low quality, lazy, and bad games because of so much shovelware. But I do think that some games lumped into this same category are just from people with good intentions who might just lack the experience, knowledge, immediate skills, and maybe the patience to do better.
I do think that using the RTP bothers more of the people that use RPG Maker themselves then people who have never touched RPG Maker. And to a lesser extent, people who play a LOT of games and therefore see the same thing over and over again.
But there are very successful game series out there that use the same assets as part of the series and they are much beloved for many reasons. The same assets don't change that. It is the other aspects of the game that people end up being critical of as they change or evolve from installment to installment.
The thing about RPG Maker (at least MZ and MV in my experience) is that the engine is so versatile that you can make almost anything you want if you are willing to put in the effort. And you can easily go outside the traditional RM style.
You say your strength is writing. I know that in MZ or MV, you could easily (relative) make a text-based, choose your own adventure (CYOA) type game that wouldn't have to use the RTP at all. Then you would be focusing almost exclusively on the story.
With that same concept, you could learn to do things that go beyond the typical CYOA model and have engaging interactions with say treasure chests that are trapped and locked. Or with various skill checks.
You could even incorporate detailed character generation with whatever aspects you wanted that end up being used in the CYOA model. You could take things that you really like about other RPGs and incorporate them into a primarily text-based interaction. Or with selection of pathways on a map.
And there are TONS of free assets available so you could do more of a picture-based presentation. And there is a lot of free music tracks out there too.
I think there are a ton of things you can do that don't require any RTP assets. It just requires ingenuity and being willing to learn how to do what you want to do.
Also, as a player, I couldn't care less if someone uses the RTP. I am more interested in the game play loop.
So, that brings up a different issue. For example, I find the default combat in RPG Maker to be less than satisfying. It really doesn't appeal to me. So, for me, having default combat is more of a turn off than RTP assets.
Anyway, I think others have given good context of why there is some animosity towards the RTP in general. But I also think you can do pretty much anything you want with the RM engine (at least MZ and MV) so you can be very creative in making a more unique game, whether you use RTP assets or not.
Good luck on whatever you decide to do!

Canned_Dinosaur said:
This is a very good point. And it kind of ties into Avery's earlier comment:
RTP maps will look a whole lot better just by clearing up the tile sheet to make some room to shift things like shelves 24 pixels along the Y-axis. It's minimal effort and you really really won't be using all the default B~E offers.
Click to expand...
Yep.  I've seen (and played) several RPG maker games with 100% custom assets before, but the mapping was just atrocious.  It was hard to know what was walkable in a couple of them.  Or, what was a "point of interest", or even "what the expected path was".
There's also a lot of "clutter" everyone adds to their maps, as if every third tile needs to have some doodad or decoration in it.  Like... negative space is important, too.  It's okay to have maps where "there's a chunk of just nothing different right here".
Is an empty desert with just two repeating tiles more interesting with the RTP or with a custom tileset?
If you can't map for crap, then it doesn't matter HOW PRETTY the assets you're using are.  The end result in the same.

posts.author: vigamanufacture
posts.body: RTP isn’t the problem... it’s just the office furniture of RPG Maker: bland, overused, but functional. People hate it because they’ve seen the same desks a thousand times, not because desks don’t work. If you’re fine with it, use it. Just make sure the story and gameplay give people a reason to hang around the office space. Maybe you're overthinking it. Honestly, if you approach map design like furnishing an office space, half the complaints will come from people who just don’t like seeing the same motivational poster every day.
